body_ar:
سائلة عن مرض (السَّل المَصْ) الشعبي وعندها قرن كبش وفيه حكمة سوداء ومعه تزلوميت، فالقرن يدخل في ماء ويشربه المصاب بالسَّل، فيشفى بإذن الله، وأما التزلوميت فتستعمل للمرأة التي استعصى عليها النفاس فما هو حكم الشرع في ذلك مع العلم أنها تستخدمه لمنافع المسلمين وهي تعلم عدم مضرته أو نفعه إلا بإذن الله؟

أن هذه الرقى كانت قديمة وكانت من أمر الجاهلية فقال النبي (ص): «اعرضوا علي رقاكم» فما كان فيها فيه تعظيم لله وذكر له أقره النبي (ص)، وما كان غير ذلك رده ونهى عنه، فكل ما لا يعرف الإنسان معناه لا يحل له الرقية به،

وبالنسبة لهذه الأمور المجسمات كالقرون وما يسمى بالتزلوميت ونحو ذلك لا يحل استعماله لأن الإنسان لا يدري ما فيه، وإذا دراه فهو أمور ظاهرها مثل ظاهر السحر لأنها مجسمات وأمور من هذا القبيل، فلذلك هذا النوع يضر ولا ينفع، وما يشاهد منه من النفع العاجل كالشفاء من مرض من الأمراض إنما هو فتنة لأن الإنسان سيتعلق به ويظن أنه يشفي أو ينفع فهو فتنة يفتن الله بها،

ونحن الآن ننتظر الدجال فعلينا أن نحذر من مثل هذه الأمور، فإذا كان الإنسان يحذر فتنة المسيح الدجال فليعلم أن الدجال يحيي الموتى، يناديهم فيقومون من قبورهم، ويمر بالقرية الخربة فتتبعه كنوزها كيعاسيب النحل، ويأتي أهل قرية وهم مسنتون في غاية الجهد فيصدقونه فيأمر السماء فتمطر ويأمر الأرض فتنبت، فتروح عليهم مواشيهم أسمن ما كانت ضروعا، ويمر على أهل قرية مخصبين فيكذبونه، فيأمر السماء فتمسك ويأمر الأرض فتقحل فتروح عليهم مواشيهم وهي أشد ما تكون لأواء،

فإذا عرفنا هذا وعرفنا أن هذه الأمور المشاهدات الدنيوية إنما هي فتن يجريها الله تعالى كما يجري أشد منها على يد المسيح الدجال، فعلى الإنسان أن لا يغتر بها وأن يعلم أن الفتن موجودة، وأن تقليد الإنسان في اتباعها، وشهادته بأن القضية هي مجرد مشاهدة أن هذا شربه فلان فبرئ وعلق على فلانة فبرئت، فهذا النوع إنما هو من الفتن التي على الإنسان أن يحذرها لأنه لو كان كل من يبرئ مريضا يتبع لكان الدجال أحق بهذا فهو يحيي الموتى، فلذلك لا بد من الحذر غاية الحذر من هذا النوع ومن خطره العقدي المؤثر على عقائد الناس،

ولنعلم أن الله سبحانه وتعالى آتانا ما فيه الشفاء والنور، فأنزل علينا هذا القرآن المبين الذي لا يأتيه الباطل من بين يديه ولا من خلفه تنزيل من حكيم حميد، وهو حبل الله المتين وصراطه المستقيم، من تمسك به عصم، ومن تركه من جبار قصم الله ظهره، وقد قال الله تعالى: { وَنُنَزِّلُ مِنَ الْقُرْآَنِ مَا هُوَ شِفَاءٌ وَرَحْمَةٌ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ} وقال: {وَإِذَا قَرَأْتَ الْقُرْآَنَ جَعَلْنَا بَيْنَكَ وَبَيْنَ الَّذِينَ لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالْآَخِرَةِ حِجَابًا مَسْتُورًا وَجَعَلْنَا عَلَى قُلُوبِهِمْ أَكِنَّةً أَنْ يَفْقَهُوهُ وَفِي آَذَانِهِمْ وَقْرًا وَإِذَا ذَكَرْتَ رَبَّكَ فِي الْقُرْآَنِ وَحْدَهُ وَلَّوْا عَلَى أَدْبَارِهِمْ نُفُورًا} وقال تعالى: { وَلَوْ أَنَّ قُرْآَنًا سُيِّرَتْ بِهِ الْجِبَالُ أَوْ قُطِّعَتْ بِهِ الْأَرْضُ أَوْ كُلِّمَ بِهِ الْمَوْتَى بَلْ لِلَّهِ الْأَمْرُ جَمِيعًا} فلذلك علينا أن نكتفي بكتاب الله تعالى، وأن نلتمس فيه الهدى، وأن نحذر من هذه الشواغل التي تشغل عنه.
body_en:
A woman asks about the folk illness (al-sall al-maṣṣ). She has a ram's horn with a black ḥikmah in it, and with it a tazlūmīt. The horn is put into water and the one afflicted with al-sall drinks it and is cured, by God's leave. As for the tazlūmīt, it is used for a woman whose post-natal period has become obstructed. What is the ruling of the Sharia on that, bearing in mind that she uses it for the benefit of Muslims and knows that it neither harms nor benefits except by God's leave?

These incantations (ruqā) are old, and were part of the business of the age of ignorance. The Prophet, upon whom be peace, said: 'Present your incantations to me.' Whatever in them contained the magnification of God and remembrance of Him, the Prophet, upon whom be peace, confirmed; and whatever was otherwise, he rejected and forbade. So everything whose meaning a person does not know, it is not lawful for him to use as an incantation.

As for these physical objects — such as horns, and what is called the tazlūmīt, and the like — it is not lawful to use them, because a person does not know what is in them; and if he does know, they are things whose outward appearance is like the outward appearance of sorcery, because they are physical objects and matters of that sort. This kind of thing therefore harms and does not benefit. And whatever immediate benefit is observed from it, such as recovery from one illness or another, is only a trial, because a person will become attached to it and suppose that it heals or benefits. It is a trial by which God tries people.

We are now awaiting the Dajjal, so we must be on our guard against things of this kind. If a person is to be on his guard against the trial of the False Messiah, let him know that the Dajjal brings the dead to life: he calls them and they rise from their graves; he passes by the ruined village and its treasures follow him like swarms of bees; he comes to the people of a village who are in drought and in the utmost distress, and they believe him, so he commands the sky and it rains, and commands the earth and it brings forth growth, and their livestock come home to them in the evening with their udders fuller than they have ever been; and he passes by the people of a village who are in plenty, and they call him a liar, so he commands the sky and it withholds, and commands the earth and it goes barren, and their livestock come home to them in the evening in the worst hardship they have ever known.

So when we know this, and know that these worldly things that are seen are only trials that God, exalted, brings about — just as He brings about what is far graver than them at the hand of the False Messiah — then a person must not be deceived by them, and must know that trials exist. A person's following them without examination, and his testimony that the matter is simply something observed — that so-and-so drank this and recovered, and it was hung on such-and-such a woman and she recovered — this kind of thing is only one of the trials a person must be on his guard against; for if everyone who cures a sick person were to be followed, the Dajjal would have the better claim to that, since he brings the dead to life. Hence the utmost caution is required against this kind of thing, and against its danger to creed, which affects what people believe.

And let us know that God, glorified and exalted, has given us that in which there is healing and light, and has sent down upon us this clear Qur'an, which falsehood does not approach from before it or from behind it, a revelation from One All-Wise, Praiseworthy. It is God's firm rope and His straight path: whoever holds fast to it is preserved, and whoever abandons it — any tyrant who does so — God breaks his back. God, exalted, has said: {And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers} (Sūrat al-Isrāʾ 17:82). And He said: {And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a concealed veil; and We have placed coverings over their hearts, lest they understand it, and in their ears a deafness. And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an, they turn their backs in aversion} (Sūrat al-Isrāʾ 17:45–46). And He, exalted, said: {And if there were a Qur'an by which the mountains were moved, or the earth were cloven apart, or the dead were spoken to — rather, to God belongs the affair entirely} (Sūrat al-Raʿd 13:31). So we must content ourselves with the Book of God, exalted, and seek guidance in it, and beware of these preoccupations that divert us from it.

options: al-sall al-maṣṣ — a folk illness name, left untranslated
a wasting illness known in local folk medicine as al-sall al-maṣṣ
consumption (tuberculosis) as named in Mauritanian folk medicine
flags.note: Hassaniya folk-medicine term; the questioner marks it as popular usage (الشعبي) and puts it in brackets herself. السل on its own is consumption/tuberculosis, but المص ('the sucking') is a local qualifier of unknown extension, so identifying it with tuberculosis would be a guess. Left untranslated pending the Sheikh's office.

flags.context: وعندها قرن كبش وفيه حكمة سوداء ومعه تزلوميت … وأما التزلوميت فتستعمل للمرأة التي استعصى عليها النفاس
options: tazlūmīt — a Mauritanian amulet object, left untranslated
a charm or talisman known as tazlūmīt
flags.note: Hassaniya dialect term for a physical object used in folk healing. The Sheikh treats it as a مجسم (a physical object) alongside horns, but neither he nor the questioner describes its form. Any English gloss would state more than the source does.

flags.context: وعندها قرن كبش وفيه حكمة سوداء
options: a black ḥikmah — an object placed inside the horn; sense uncertain
flags.note: IMPORTANT: this is not the usul term ḥikmah ('underlying wisdom') in the glossary. Here it names a physical thing inside the ram's horn. The referent is not established by the source and has deliberately not been guessed.

flags.context: وأما التزلوميت فتستعمل للمرأة التي استعصى عليها النفاس
options: a woman whose post-natal period (nifās) has become obstructed
a woman whose childbirth has become difficult
a woman whose post-natal bleeding will not stop
flags.note: استعصى عليها النفاس can point to obstructed labour, to retained lochia, or to bleeding that will not cease. The Arabic does not decide between them, and the medical referent matters for how the fatwa reads. Left deliberately general in the English.

translator_notes: Qur'anic renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic.

The words 'لا يأتيه الباطل من بين يديه ولا من خلفه تنزيل من حكيم حميد' are Qur'an (Sūrat Fuṣṣilat 41:42) woven into the Sheikh's own prose without quotation marks in the source. They have been left unbraced in the English, matching the source, rather than promoted to a marked quotation.
The description of the Dajjal reproduces the wording of the well-known long hadith of al-Nawwas ibn Samʿan, but the Sheikh gives no narrator, collection or grading here, and none has been supplied.
لا يحل is rendered 'it is not lawful', not 'it is not permissible', so that 'permissible' remains reserved for mubāḥ per the five-rulings table.

The Sheikh's ruling on the objects is given as لا يحل استعماله ('it is not lawful to use them'), and his ruling on incantations of unknown meaning likewise. He does not use ḥarām or makrūh here, and no ruling word has been supplied for him.
